Learning Objectives
Assess the clinical presentation and evaluation of clavicular injuries, including sternoclavicular
and acromioclavicular injuries, in pediatric and adolescent patients.
Review pertinent treatment options and outcomes associated with the management of
clavicular fractures and sternoclavicular, and acromioclavicular injuries in pediatric and
adolescent patients.
Outline the complications associated with the treatment of pediatric and adolescent patients
with a clavicle injury.

Overview
Clavicular fractures are common in all pediatric age groups, account for 90% of obstetric
fractures, and often are associated with brachial plexus palsy.1 (Resource 1)
Presence of a clavicular fracture at birth has prognostic value in the recovery of a brachial
plexus palsy.2
Clavicular fractures may be confused with congenital pseudarthrosis of the clavicle.
Congenital pseudarthrosis results from a congenital failure of fusion of the medial and lateral
ossification centers of the clavicle; may be related to external compression by the subclavian
artery against the developing clavicle on the right side, except in cases of situs inversus.
Typical findings include presence at birth, although prominence of a bump often increases
with age; right side location; no pain; and radiographs that demonstrate convexity of the
ends of the nonfused portions of the clavicle (Video 1).
Video 1 Rudzki JR: Clavicle trauma: Distal clavicle fractures & SC injuries, from McKee MD, mod:
Clavicle trauma: From midshaft fractures in contact athletes to distal clavicle fractures and
acromioclavicular joint injuries. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, New Orleans, LA, March 6-10, 2019.

Medial clavicle injuries often are high-energy injuries.

Anterior displacement is more common.
Lateral clavicle injuries
Most are low-grade injuries with minimal displacement.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
Clavicle is first bone to ossify and last to close.1
The clavicle has two ossification centers located on the medial and lateral ends. These
ossification centers are specific locations in the bone where the bone ossifies during
longitudinal growth. If an ossification center closes, it is no longer visible on radiographs, and
longitudinal growth has completed (ie, the growth plate has closed).
Double curve
Convex forward in its medial two-thirds
Concave forward in the lateral one-third
Medial clavicle is the last long bone to ossify (age 23 to 25 years).
Many medial clavicle fractures are physeal fractures.
Strong costoclavicular and sternoclavicular ligaments generally remain in continuity during
an injury, with a thick periosteal sleeve.7,8
Posteriorly displaced fractures or dislocations may impinge on the mediastinum, including
the great vessels, esophagus, and trachea.
Lateral clavicle ossifies at approximately age 20 years.
Lateral clavicle injuries are more likely to also be physeal fractures.
Coracoclavicular ligaments (trapezoid and conoid) are likely to remain intact to the thick
periosteal sleeve.
May be confused with an acromioclavicular joint dislocation, which is rare in children

Injury Classification
Whether injuries to the clavicle are medial, midshaft, or lateral, the anatomy of the
young, injured patient precludes using data from adult injuries in the management of
pediatric clavicular injuries. Anatomic considerations include the robust healing
properties of young bone, a thickened periosteum, and physeal injury (in contrast to
ligament injury) on the proximal and distal ends of the clavicle. In general, injuries in a


Outcomes
In 2003, Waters et al19 reported on a series of posterior sternoclavicular injuries in
children. This series was a retrospective review of 13 patients (mean age, 14.6 years)
with a follow-up of 22 months. All patients underwent surgical reduction of the medial
physeal fracture and ligament stabilization with the use of sutures. No complications
were noted; all patients had excellent outcomes. In a series of 12 boys, Tepolt et al18
reported that 25% of the posterior sternoclavicular injuries responded to closed
reduction alone, whereas the remainder of the injuries required open reduction and
stabilization. Closed reduction, if attempted, is most successful if performed within 48
hours postinjury.9 In the largest series to date, which included skeletally immature
patients with a medial clavicular injury, Lee et al17 found that one-half of the patients
had a true dislocation, whereas the other one-half had a true physeal fracture. The
success of closed reduction in this series was associated with a physeal fracture (in
contrast to a true dislocation) and performance of the reduction within 24 hours
postinjury. Also noted in this series is that 25% of the injuries were missed on initial
evaluation.

Adult literature is not applicable to pediatric and adolescent patients.
Several small series, including small comparative series with mixed outcomes, were
reported.29-31 In general, all healed with no limitation in function, motion, or strength. Rarely,
poor outcomes were reported to be related to symptomatic malunion in nonsurgically
managed fractures.

In response to the adult literature and despite the paucity of data in the pediatric and
adolescent literature, an increase in the surgical management of adolescent clavicle
fractures has been observed.32 A recent, multicenter, large cohort study (n = 907) of

demonstrated no differences in patient-reported outcomes between surgically and
nonsurgically managed fractures (assessed via American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons
Shoulder scores; Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand questionnaire scores;
EQ-5D questionnaire scores; and EQ-5D visual analogue scale scores). Although
surgically treated patients experienced more returns to the operating room for
hardware removal, no differences were observed in complications or the rates of
nonunion between the surgically and nonsurgically managed fractures. This unpublished
study also evaluated differences in displaced and nondisplaced fractures and did not
report a considerable difference in surgical management.

Duplication of the clavicle may be observed and is associated with prominent bump.34,35
Duplication of the clavicle occurs if the radiographs demonstrate the appearance of two
clavicles on the lateral side of the shoulder during healing. The appearance of the duplication
is caused by the early callus formation and will remodel to a single clavicle.
Outcome is excellent and is not associated with amount of fracture displacement.36

Suture fixation via suspensory technique
Hook plate construct
